items.title: What Will It Take to Be Confident About Inflation? | Investing.com
items.excerpt: Risk management, the Fed’s main rationale in September, points to another rate hike next week. Markets put the odds at one in five. ... A question I was asked repeatedly this year on Bloomberg: “Are you confident inflation is going back to 2%?” Early in the year, I said yes; the temporary boost from energy prices and tariffs would wane, delivering the necessary disinflation. By the end of the summer, I was much less confident. In September, I shifted to favoring modest rate hikes as insurance against persistently elevated inflation. Risk management was a signature approach of the Powell Fed and was also the most common reason given in the FOMC minutes for the September rate increase. ... Information since the September meeting has underscored the upside risks to inflation, while the labor market has remained in balance. Long lags between changes in the policy rate and their effects on inflation argue for adjusting policy sooner rather than later. Other considerations, such as higher long-term interest rates, the timing of the midterm election, and the potential for a market surprise, are insufficient to justify a hold in October. Currently, futures markets imply less than a 20% chance of a rate increase next week, partly reflecting patient messages from Fed leadership in recent weeks. The case for a rate hike is stronger than the odds suggest. ... The September CPI offered little to build confidence in disinflation. First, the upside surprise was broad-based, unlike in August, when it was concentrated in wireless services. Second, while energy drove the 0.6% headline increase in September, core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.33%, an annualized rate of about 4%. Finally, the disinflation over the three-month horizon (orange line below), which Fed Governor Waller had highlighted as a possible inflection point before the August CPI, reversed. ... The September PPI shows even more pricing pressure in the pipeline. The direct effect of higher energy prices was as clear in the PPI as in the CPI, and the PPI also shows those energy costs feeding into non-energy goods and services, the second-round effects. Prices that U.S. businesses charge for transportation and warehousing services (blue line) continued to rise sharply in September and are now increasing at a pace last seen in 2022. items.title: September CPI Report: Inflation Hits 3.7%, Markets Wobble
items.excerpt: The September CPI report came in hotter than anyone wanted. Inflation ran at 3.7% year over year through September, the Labor Department said on October 14 — a touch above what economists expected, and a fresh reminder that the fight against rising prices isn’t over yet. But investors didn’t just worry about the Federal Reserve this time. They worried about whether Wall Street’s giant AI spending spree will ever pay for itself. ... Here’s the fear underneath it all. The AI industry is spending like there’s no tomorrow: chips, buildings, power plants, data centers — much of it funded by debt. With the 10-year Treasury yielding above 5% and mortgages near 7.5%, money isn’t cheap anymore. The September CPI report only added to worries that borrowing costs will stay high. ... After the hot September CPI report, futures traders briefly piled into bets on a rate hike at the Fed’s October 27-28 meeting. Fed officials spent the week talking them down. ... “We are more likely than not to need additional adjustments, but the timing of those adjustments to me is something we’re still deliberating,” San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly told Reuters on October 14. “I don’t feel urgent that we have to decide with a limited set of information. I think we have the time that we need.” ... The policy rate sits at 3.75% to 4.00% after the Fed raised it a quarter point in September — its first hike since 2023. New York Fed President John Williams, the committee’s vice chair, reaffirmed that one more hike in 2026 may fit, adding he has “no reason to believe” more would be needed in 2027. Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari said he’s “open-minded” about timing. The message from all of them: not October. Probably December, if at all. ... Confusion after the September CPI report sent investors sprinting for safety. The 10-year Treasury yield, which climbed above 5.3% last week, dropped to around 5.1% — its biggest weekly decline since February. Bond prices rise when yields fall, and money that fled tech stocks poured into government debt. ... October’s story is really two stories. The September CPI report confirms inflation refuses to die — 3.7% is a long way from the Fed’s 2% target — and the market’s faith in the AI spending boom is cracking. The Fed has time, as Daly put it. Investors, nursing record valuations and record borrowing costs at the same time, may not. The next few weeks — the October FOMC meeting, earnings season, and November inflation data — will decide whether this was a scare or the start of something uglier.

items.excerpt: Early snow is already dusting the northeasternmost US state of Maine, where a canny 73-year-old Republican senator is having to run the race of her life to help save Donald Trump's party from being frozen out of power nationwide. Susan Collins has held her Senate seat for three decades, becoming a near immovable fixture in the state's political landscape. But with President Trump deeply unpopular nationwide and Mainers furious about surging fuel prices ahead of winter, Collins's Democratic challenger is eying an upset -- and a chance to make his party's outside bid to regain the Senate a reality. The stakes are enormous in the race between Collins and logger-turned-politician Troy Jackson, as Maine is crucial for any Democratic path to a US Senate majority. While Democrats are forecast to win the House of Representatives in the November 3 midterms, they would need to clinch the Senate too if they want to stop Trump's right-wing agenda in its tracks, including his power to nominate Supreme Court justices. About one-third of Maine's voters are unaffiliated with either party. Because independents generally are opposed to Trump nationwide, that could work to Jackson's advantage. Most voters interviewed by AFP agreed that Collins had done well in funneling federal funding back to Maine over the years and that 58-year-old newcomer Jackson would not be so successful. But like many Mainers, retired teacher Louisa Beckett believes a perfect storm of national setbacks -- cost-of-living hikes, the Iran war, and allegations of massive Trump corruption -- could finally sink Collins. ... 2020 she trailed her Democratic challenger in pre-election polling. items.title: Poll: Voters Oppose Political Control of Grant Making
items.excerpt: Poll: Voters Oppose Political Control of Grant Making October 21, 2026 # Poll: Battleground Voters Oppose Political Control of Grant Making By Kathryn Palmer Photo illustration by Justin Morrison/Inside Higher Ed | SDI Productions/E+/Getty Images Ahead of the midterm elections Nov. 3, a new poll shows that voters in some Midwestern battleground states don’t approve of the federal government’s plans to assert more political control over the federal grant-making process. Earlier this month, United for Cures Action surveyed 1,200 registered voters in Iowa, Kansas, and Ohio, all of which Republican President Donald Trump won in 2024. According to the survey, published last week, 76 percent of voters in those states oppose the Office of Management and Budget’s proposal to overhaul the grant-approval process, including at the National Institutes of Health, the National Science Foundation and other federal agencies that send millions in research funding to universities each year. Right now, peer reviewers at those agencies make the final decision on who is awarded a grant. But under the proposal (which advocacy groups, including United for Cures, have opposed), political appointees would have the final say on awards, which could be canceled at their discretion. Strong voter opposition to the proposal extends across geographic and party lines. According to the poll, 77 percent of voters in Iowa and Kansas oppose, along with 75 percent in Ohio. Across all three states, 88 percent of Democrats, 82 percent of independents and 64 percent of Republicans oppose it. The poll also found that 64 percent believe the federal government spends too little on medical research, while 91 percent believe that federally funded medical research has had a “great deal” or “some” impact on finding breakthrough cures and treatments. The “bottom line,” United for Cures Action wrote in a memo about the poll, is “Voters clearly do not want increased political interference with federal grants from EITHER party.” ## Written By Kathryn Palmer

items.excerpt: Entertainment News (10/21/26) - BusinessWorld Online # Entertainment News (10/21/26) PRODUCER, songwriter, and multi-instrumentalist Ziv has teamed up with rising P-pop girl group VVINK for “Trisikulo,” a pop track on the familiar third-wheel experience. October 20, 2026 | 6:06 pm ## Ziv, VVINK release collaboration PRODUCER, songwriter, and multi-instrumentalist Ziv has teamed up with rising P-pop girl group VVINK for “Trisikulo,” a pop track on the familiar third-wheel experience. Released under Sony Music Entertainment, it is built around Filipino wordplay that links a tricycle’s three wheels to the feeling of being the extra person in someone else’s love story. The song was co-written by Ziv alongside Paolo Benjamin Guico of Filipino folk-pop band Ben&Ben and Angelika Samantha Ortiz, one of the songwriters behind BINI’s hit “Pantropiko.” The mixing was also done by Jacques Jenkins and mastering by Luna Tebbs. The track is out now on all digital music streaming platforms. ## *Love in Disguise* premieres on Prime Video *LOVE in Disguise*, a Korean series based on the hit web novel *Why Don’t You Know It’s a Girl?*, has premiered on Prime Video. It is directed by Park Dhan-hee and stars Yim Si Wan, Seorina, Kim Junghyun, and Yeonwoo. The genre-blending romance is exclusively seen on Prime Video in the Philippines and in more than 240 countries and territories worldwide. ## Estelle Fly drops club-pop single SINGAPOREAN pop artist Estelle Fly has released “Shut It Down,” a playful club-pop single about switching off the overthinking and making the dance floor your own. Inspired by the Rihanna and Kesha songs, the new release is an invitation to let loose, dance with friends and have fun even when life feels complicated. It is out now on all digital music streaming platforms. ## Cayabyab, APO, Mitch Valdes reunion THIS holiday season, National Artist for Music Ryan Cayabyab, OPM legends APO, and performer Mitch Valdes will come together for *naRyan nAPO Kami*, the fourth chapter of the MaestroClass Concert Series. The shows will be held on Dec. 4, 5, and 6 at the Proscenium Theater at Rockwell Center, Makati. All shows take place at 7:30 p.m. Joined by the Ryan Cayabyab Singers, the special Christmas chapter of the concert series brings together familiar songs, stories, and artists in a celebration that captures the warmth and spirit of a Filipino family gathering. Tickets are available directly at the Proscenium Theater website via *https://prosceniumtheater.com/* and at the Power Plant Mall Cinema. ## *Amir* gets international distribution GMA Pictures, GMA Public Affairs, and Brightburn Entertainment have officially locked in a partnership deal with Columbia Pictures for the distribution of the upcoming fantasy-drama film and 52 nd Metro Manila Film Festival (MMFF) finalist *Amir*. It is directed by Zig Dulay, with a script crafted by National Artist for Film and Broadcast Arts Ricky Lee alongside Anj Atienza. The film’s cast features Dennis Trillo, Argus Aspiras, Glaiza de Castro, Will Ashley, Caprice Cayetano, Epy Quizon, Joel Saracho, Ronnie Lazaro, Laila Ulao, Heath Jornales, Yasser Marta, Mad Ramos, Ethan Hariot, Hebron Ecal, and Mon Confiado. ## Rachel Chinouriri releases new album UK’s indie-pop singer-songwriter Rachel Chinouriri has released her second studio album, I think I spoke too soon, via Atlas Artists/Parlophone Records. The album expands upon the pop, indie, and rock influences that Ms. Chinouriri has long used to sketch portraits of her inner world. The album’s focus track is “Pretty girls,” which celebrates women, self-confidence, and the freedom to express oneself without fear of judgement. ## M2M 2027 world tour has Manila leg NORWEGIAN pop duo M2M have announced that their global tour *TWO* will be coming to Manila in 2027. The tour will start in March and after concerts at Mexico, Singapore, Hong Kong, and Jakarta, M2M’s global tour will reach Manila on April 2, 2027, at the Araneta Coliseum in Quezon City. Tickets will go on sale on Oct. 24 at 10 a.m. via *TicketNet.com.ph* and TicketNet outlets nationwide. items.excerpt: LAIKA has set the U.S. premiere of its highly-anticipated new film, Wildwood, at the 40th edition of AFI FEST presented by Canva on Wednesday, October 21, at the TCL Chinese Theatres in Hollywood, two days before the epic stop-motion fantasy hits theaters nationwide through Fathom Entertainment. ... The film is a long time coming: Travis Knight directs and produces from a screenplay by Chris Butler, based on the novel by Colin Meloy, which LAIKA optioned way back in 2011. Caleb Deschanel handles cinematography; Peyton Elizabeth Lee and Jacob Tremblay lead the voice cast, alongside Carey Mulligan, Academy Award winner Mahershala Ali, Angela Bassett, Awkwafina, Jake Johnson, Charlie Day, Amandla Stenberg, Jemaine Clement, Maya Erskine, Tantoo Cardinal, Tom Waits and Richard E. Grant. ... AFI FEST runs October 21-25 at the TCL Chinese Theatres, with Red Carpet Premieres, Special Screenings, World Cinema, Documentaries and Short Films. The full lineup will be unveiled September 29, individual tickets go on sale October 3, and passes are available now at FEST.AFI.com. The festival is an Academy Awards qualifying festival for the Live Action, Animated and Documentary Short Film categories.
